}}'''Marc Julia'''  (23 October 1922 – 29 June 2010) was a French chemist and the winner of the 1990 CNRS Gold Medal<ref>{{cite web | url =  http://www.cnrs.fr/en/research/awards/goldmedals.htm | title =  CNRS Gold medalists | access-date =  2011-03-16 | archive-url =  https://web.archive.org/web/20190503025425/https://www.cnrs.fr/en/research/awards/goldmedals.htm | archive-date = 2019-05-03 | url-status = dead }}</ref> in chemistry.<ref name="angew">{{cite journal | last1 = Chottard | first1 = Jean-Claude | last2 = Lallemand | first2 = Jean-Yves | last3 = Mansuy | first3 = Daniel | last4 = Verpeaux | first4 = Jean-Noël | title = Marc Julia (1922-2010) | journal = Angewandte Chemie International Edition | volume = 49 | issue = 48 | pages = 9038–9039 | year = 2010 | doi = 10.1002/anie.201006207| doi-access = free }}</ref>  He discovered the [[Julia olefination]]  reaction in 1973.<ref>{{cite journal | doi =10.1016/S0040-4039(01)87348-2 | title =Syntheses a l'aide de sulfones v(+)- methode de synthese generale de doubles liaisons. | year =1973 | last1 =Julia | first1 =M | journal =Tetrahedron Letters | volume =14 | issue =49 | pages =4833–4836 }}</ref>

==Biography==
Julia was born in 1922 in Paris as son of the renowned mathematician [[Gaston Julia]]. Julia studied physics at the [[École Normale Supérieure]]. After receiving his diploma he joined the group of [[Ian Heilbron]] and [[David G. Jones]] at the [[Imperial College London]] where he received his first PhD in 1948.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Gay|first1=Hannah|last2=Griffith|first2=W. P.|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/1012640130|title=The Chemistry Department at Imperial College, London : a history, 1845-2000|date=2017|isbn=978-1-78326-974-7|pages=227|oclc=1012640130}}</ref> Back to France he changed his subject to chemistry and subsequently received his second PhD for work with {{ill|Georges Dupont (chemist)|lt=Georges Dupont|fr|Georges Dupont (chimiste)}}.<ref name="angew"/>
